strengths: The paper raises an upstream, well-motivated question — where to partition an edge-cloud model for intrinsic MIA resistance — rather than proposing yet another incremental perturbation-based defence. The reframing that depth matters only insofar as it enables a feature-to-decision representational transition is a genuinely useful insight for the collaborative-inference privacy literature.

The work couples an information-theoretic analysis (upper bounds on H(Z) via maximum-entropy and determinant–trace inequalities, yielding lower bounds on H(X|Z) with a continuous-to-discrete bridge in Appendices B–C) with a practical, computable criterion (intra-class radius R²_c) and an automatic GPZ-location algorithm (Algorithm 1) validated against empirical transition zones (Table 5), including dimension-normalization to avoid artifacts and three stability checks.

The experimental evaluation is extensive for a vision setting: four architectures (IR-152, ResNet-50, VGG19, ViT), multiple datasets (CIFAR-10, FaceScrub, KMNIST/MNIST/EMNIST), four metrics (MSE/PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS), attacks on models trained with and without label smoothing, stress tests via entropy-enhanced representations and strengthened inversion models (Tables 3, 4), and a deployment-cost analysis (Appendix I) that connects the privacy analysis to latency/energy/communication trade-offs.

The training-dynamics analysis of R²_c (Appendices E–F), including the first-order gradient analysis, the O(α) prediction-independent residual under label smoothing, and the gradient-norm lower bound, is carefully derived and empirically corroborated (e.g., VGG block-wise tables), and the paper is commendably honest about the 'Neural Vortex' being a metaphorical explanatory concept rather than a formal mechanism (Appendix G).

Limitations are discussed candidly: data-dependence of the transition, the ViT negative result with a cautious hypothesis about Transformers, and explicit scope clarification of what the evaluation is intended to show (Appendix J).
weaknesses: The theoretical core is looser than the framing suggests. The bounds are Gaussian-maximum-entropy surrogates; the decisive 'surrogate gap' (Eq. 8) is argued heuristically (the paper itself concedes d and D are often only 1–4× apart and κ_Δ may be loose/vacuous). More importantly, the link from a larger lower bound on H(X|Z) to actual MIA resistance is correlational: the empirical 'high-quality reconstruction' threshold (MSE < 0.02) is ad hoc, and no formal statement connects the bound to attack success of any attacker class.

There is an element of circularity in GPZ validation: the transition zone is partly designated post hoc as 'the region just before clear MSE divergence' (Sec. 4.2), and the R²_c-based locator is validated against attack outcomes (Table 5) rather than against an independent ground truth, so the theory-driven criterion partially shares the same evidence as the attack-driven one.

Empirical coverage is narrow relative to the generality of the claims: all experiments are on 64×64 images, small datasets (CIFAR-10, FaceScrub, handwriting datasets), and models trained from scratch; no pretrained ImageNet-scale models, no text/LMs (explicitly deferred), and the ViT finding rests on a single small 6-layer configuration. The '4×' and '66%' headline numbers are averages over these settings with enhanced-attack variants that are themselves somewhat ad hoc compositions of modules.

The label-smoothing/Neural Vortex findings substantially overlap with known results (Struppek et al., 2024 on LS and inversion; neural collapse on intra-class compactness), and the paper's added value there — a training-dynamics explanation — is supported by first-order analysis whose assumptions (coherent T-term signs, bounded singular values) are plausible but not directly verified empirically.

Reproducibility is weakened by the reference to code and architectures 'available on GitHub' with no actual URL or artifact included, and key details (exact transition-zone designations, hyperparameters) are spread across an unusually fragmented appendix structure; presentation is dense and terminology-heavy (GPZ, Neural Vortex, three overlapping ways to locate the zone), which burdens the reader.

strengths: The paper addresses an upstream, under-explored question in collaborative inference security: where to partition the model rather than how to perturb transmitted features. This reframing is arguably more useful than another incremental defence, and the paper is explicit about its scope (Appendix J 'Scope clarification').

The empirical coverage is extensive: four architectures (IR-152, ResNet-50, VGG19, ViT), seven datasets, multiple evaluation metrics (MSE, PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS) beyond the pixel-wise metrics common in prior MIA work, stress tests with entropy-enhanced features and strengthened inversion models, plus a genuinely useful deployment-overhead analysis (Appendix I) covering latency, communication, and energy.

The theoretical machinery, while built on standard results, is derived carefully and completely in Appendices A–F, including an exact continuous-to-discrete entropy bridge (Lemma B.1) that honestly acknowledges FP32 non-uniformity, and stability checks for the R²c-based GPZ location algorithm (sampling/seed/condition stability).

The limitations discussion is unusually honest: the ViT negative result is reported rather than hidden, the possibility that decision-level resistance may fail under in-distribution auxiliary data is acknowledged (Appendix H.7), and the bounds are explicitly flagged as potentially vacuous (Appendix C 'Practical note').

Practically actionable guidance emerges from the analysis (e.g., VGG-family backbones reach a GPZ with ~2.5% edge parameters vs. ~78% for ResNet-style models), which is more concrete than most analysis-driven papers in this space.
weaknesses: The central theoretical contribution is a chain of loose upper bounds whose practical content is questionable. The authors themselves concede that κ∆(m) is an 'upper envelope' that 'may be loose and may become vacuous in absolute value' (Appendix C). The derivation of the feature-level bound applies the Gaussian maximum-entropy result to the marginal Z without conditioning on Y, while the decision-level bound conditions on Y — so the claimed 'abrupt rise' in the H(X|Z) lower bound partly follows from an asymmetry in the analysis (conditioning) rather than from a measured property of representations. No empirical validation of bound tightness is provided.

The 'representational transition' that the entire paper rests on is never rigorously defined. Feature-level vs. decision-level is characterized informally (spatial resolution collapse, CLS-token concentration), and the GPZ is in part identified 'post hoc from MIA outcomes' — which introduces a circularity risk: the theory predicts resistance, but the transition zone is partly delimited by where resistance appears. Table 5 shows the R²c-based active location for VGG19 (26→30) disagrees with the empirically observed transition (17→26), undermining the claim that R²c reliably predicts the boundary.

The headline empirical results (4× MSE, 66%) are confounded by inversion difficulty at low spatial resolution. In the residual case, the sharp MSE rise occurs exactly when the representation drops to 4×4; it is well known that decoding from such heavily downsampled features is hard for any decoder, regardless of any 'transition'. The paper does not disentangle intrinsic information loss (DPI, which holds trivially for any deeper layer) from the specific representational-transition mechanism it posits — a stronger attack with a generative prior or diffusion-based inversion (e.g., Chen et al., 2024, cited but not compared) could plausibly erode the claimed decision-level resistance.

The 'Neural Vortex' is largely a relabeling of known label-smoothing effects. The training-dynamics analysis (Appendix E–F) is competent first-order sensitivity work, but the phenomenon — that LS alters feature geometry and MIA susceptibility — was already established by Struppek et al. (2024), which the paper itself cites. The dramatic terminology overstates the novelty of what is fundamentally an application of existing observations to the partitioning setting, and the appendix itself concedes the term is 'metaphorical' and not a formal mechanism.

Experimental scope is narrow relative to the generality of the claims: all experiments are on 64×64 images with CIFAR/FaceScrub-scale models. Claims like 'depth is sufficient only insofar as it enables a representational transition, whereas the transition is necessary' are stated as general principles but tested only in this regime; the text-domains extension is left as a 'cautious hypothesis'.

Reproducibility is incomplete: multiple code links in the manuscript are left blank ('available on GitHub.'), a significant gap for a paper whose main artifacts are empirical validations of a criterion.

Presentation relies heavily on branded terminology (Golden Partition Zone, Neural Vortex) that adds no technical content and can obscure the actual contributions: (i) depth alone does not guarantee inversion resistance, (ii) a within-class radius correlates with inversion difficulty, (iii) label smoothing contracts this radius. Each of these could be stated and defended more plainly.

strengths: The paper addresses an upstream, practically relevant question—where to partition an edge–cloud model for intrinsic resistance to model inversion—rather than proposing yet another perturbation-based defence; this framing is well motivated and clearly positioned against prior work (Sec. 1, Appendix J).

The empirical study is broad and thorough: four architectures (IR-152, ResNet-50, VGG19, ViT), seven datasets, multiple metrics (MSE/PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS), enhanced inversion attackers (feature augmentation and attention-based strengthening), stress tests against stronger attacks, and a detailed deployment-cost analysis (Appendix I) including latency, communication, energy, and edge-parameter footprint.

The R²c-based algorithm for actively locating the transition zone (Appendix D) is a concrete, deployable tool, and the authors perform genuine stability checks (sampling-seed, training-seed, and LS-condition stability) rather than relying on a single run.

The first-order analysis of how one-hot vs. label-smoothed supervision reshapes the intra-class radius (Eqs. 10–12, Appendices E–F) is a genuinely interesting training-dynamics perspective, connecting label-distribution design to representation geometry.
The paper is commendably honest about the limitations of its own theory (e.g., admitting κ_Δ can be loose or vacuous in Appendix C) and includes an impact statement and scope discussion.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claim—an 'abrupt rise in the lower bound of H(X|Z)'—is not directly validated. The bounds are standard maximum-entropy and determinant–trace surrogates, and the finite-precision correction κ_Δ is admitted to be potentially loose or vacuous; the true conditional entropy is never estimated. The 'abruptness' and the shift from σ²_feat to R²c are asserted from the surrogate gap (Eq. 8) rather than measured.

There is a degree of circularity in the validation: the 'representational transition zone' (red zones in Figs. 4–6) is designated post hoc from where MSE diverges, and then GPZ partitioning is evaluated against the same MIA outcomes. The R²c-based active location only partially matches the empirical zones (Table 5: for VGG19 it predicts 26→30/30→39 vs. the empirical 17→26/39→43), and the reconciliation is qualitative.

The 'Neural Vortex' is, by the authors' own admission (Appendix G), a metaphor rather than a formal mechanism; presenting it as a named contribution overstates its status and the label adds little analytical content beyond 'higher output entropy with tighter decision-level geometry'.

The headline numbers (4× MSE increase, 66% stronger resistance) are aggregates over heterogeneous settings; the practical resistance at the GPZ is partly confounded with loss of utility at very deep splits, and the adversary model excludes the strongest recent attacks (e.g., the diffusion-based DIA of Chen et al. 2024 is cited but not tested).

Generality is limited: all experiments are 64×64 vision models; the ViT result (no GPZ due to persistent patch tokens) suggests the framework may not transfer to Transformer/sequence models, which the authors acknowledge but this narrows the scope of the 'intrinsic resistance' claim.

The relationship to Struppek et al. (2024)—that label smoothing can catalyze MIA—is in tension with the paper's LS-based control recommendation; the resolution (feature-vs-decision level) is plausible but the deployment guidance requires care that the main text does not fully disambiguate.

Reproducibility is partially undermined: GitHub URLs are incomplete/placeholder in the manuscript, and several key quantities (e.g., layer-wise R²c trajectories that justify the transition peak) are described but not shown in the main text.
